why: Cd38 is the mouse ortholog of human CD38 and encodes CD38, a cell-surface glycoprotein with ectoenzyme activity involved in the metabolism of NAD+ and cyclic ADP-ribose. CD38 is expressed on plasma cells and various immune cells and has been associated with roles in calcium signaling and cell adhesion.

CD38 is highly expressed on malignant plasma cells in multiple myeloma, and CD38-directed antibodies are used in that disease, often combined with other agents; responses vary. Cd38-deficient mice are viable and show altered immune and metabolic responses.
applications: Humanized CD38 models, in which the human protein replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate anti-CD38 antibodies in immunocompetent mice.
Cd38 knockout mice have been used to study NAD+ metabolism and immune regulation in defined experimental settings.

why: Flt3 is the mouse ortholog of human FLT3 and encodes FLT3 (CD135), a class III receptor tyrosine kinase expressed on hematopoietic progenitor cells. Binding of FLT3 ligand promotes signaling that has been associated with proliferation and survival of early progenitors.

Activating FLT3 mutations, including internal tandem duplications, have been associated with acute myeloid leukemia, and FLT3 inhibitors are used in FLT3-mutated disease; resistance can emerge. Flt3-deficient mice are viable with reduced numbers of certain progenitor populations.
applications: Humanized FLT3 models, in which the human receptor replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate FLT3-targeted agents.
Flt3 models have been used to study hematopoiesis and FLT3-driven leukemia in defined experimental settings.

why: Msln is the mouse ortholog of human MSLN and encodes mesothelin, a GPI-anchored cell-surface glycoprotein normally expressed on mesothelial cells. Mesothelin has been associated with cell adhesion, and its normal physiological role is not fully defined.

Mesothelin is overexpressed on several solid tumors, including mesothelioma and ovarian and pancreatic cancers, and mesothelin-directed antibody–drug conjugates, CAR T cells, and antibodies have been evaluated; clinical results have varied. Msln-deficient mice are viable without an overt phenotype under standard conditions.
applications: Humanized MSLN models, in which the human protein replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate mesothelin-targeted therapeutics, including antibody–drug conjugates and cell therapies, in defined experimental settings.

why: Gpc3 is the mouse ortholog of human GPC3 and encodes glypican-3, a GPI-anchored heparan sulfate proteoglycan. Glypican-3 has been associated with regulation of cell growth and signaling during development, and loss-of-function variants are linked to an overgrowth syndrome.

Glypican-3 is expressed on most hepatocellular carcinomas with limited expression in normal adult liver, and glypican-3-directed agents, including CAR T cells and antibodies, have been evaluated; clinical results have varied. Gpc3-deficient mice show developmental overgrowth features.
applications: Humanized GPC3 models, in which the human protein replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate glypican-3-targeted therapeutics in defined experimental settings.

why: Cd3e is the mouse ortholog of human CD3E and encodes the CD3ε subunit of the T-cell receptor–CD3 complex. CD3ε contributes to assembly and surface expression of the complex and to transmission of T-cell-receptor signals.

CD3ε is the engagement point for T-cell-redirecting bispecific antibodies (T-cell engagers) used in several cancers, and anti-CD3 antibodies have other clinical uses; effects depend on the specific agent and context. Loss of CD3ε function has been associated with impaired T-cell development.
applications: Humanized CD3E models, in which the human subunit replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate T-cell-engaging bispecific antibodies in immunocompetent mice, often combined with humanization of a tumor-target antigen.
Cd3e models have been used to study T-cell-receptor signaling in defined experimental settings.

why: Mapt is the mouse ortholog of human MAPT and encodes tau, a microtubule-associated protein enriched in neurons. Tau has been associated with regulation of microtubule stability and axonal transport, and it is expressed as multiple isoforms.

Aggregated tau is a feature of Alzheimer’s disease and other tauopathies, and MAPT mutations are linked to frontotemporal dementia; tau-directed therapies are under study, though clinical results to date have been mixed. Humanized and mutant Mapt alleles have been developed to study tau biology.
applications: Humanized MAPT models, which express human tau isoforms, have been used to study tau aggregation and to evaluate tau-targeted approaches in defined experimental settings.
Mapt knockout and mutant models have been used to study tau function.

why: Lrrk2 is the mouse ortholog of human LRRK2 and encodes a large protein containing both GTPase and kinase domains. LRRK2 has been associated with regulation of vesicle trafficking, lysosomal function, and other cellular processes.

LRRK2 mutations, including the common G2019S variant, are among the more frequent genetic contributors to Parkinson’s disease, and LRRK2 kinase inhibitors are under clinical investigation. Lrrk2-deficient mice are viable and show changes in lung and kidney and in lysosomal markers.

why: Ldlr is the mouse ortholog of human LDLR and encodes the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor, a cell-surface receptor that mediates uptake of LDL particles and has been associated with regulation of plasma cholesterol.

Loss-of-function LDLR mutations cause familial hypercholesterolemia, and the LDL-receptor pathway is central to lipid-lowering therapy; agents such as statins and PCSK9 inhibitors act in part by increasing LDL-receptor activity. Ldlr-deficient mice develop elevated cholesterol and atherosclerosis on appropriate diets and are widely used in cardiovascular research.
applications: Ldlr knockout mice are widely used to study atherosclerosis and lipid metabolism. Humanized LDLR models, in which the human receptor replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to study LDL-receptor regulation and lipid-lowering agents in defined experimental settings.

why: Il5 is the mouse ortholog of human IL5 and encodes interleukin-5, a type 2 cytokine produced mainly by T helper 2 cells and group 2 innate lymphoid cells. IL-5 has been associated with the differentiation, survival, and recruitment of eosinophils.

why: Il33 is the mouse ortholog of human IL33 and encodes interleukin-33, an IL-1-family cytokine that can be released from epithelial and endothelial cells and acts as an alarmin. IL-33 signals through the receptor ST2 and has been associated with promotion of type 2 immune responses.

IL-33 is implicated in asthma and other inflammatory conditions, and IL-33- and ST2-directed antibodies are under clinical study. Il33-deficient mice are viable and show altered type 2 responses in disease models.

Il33 knockout mice have been used to study alarmin biology and type 2 immunity.
